issues.legal_issue: A land-revenue assessment scheme violates equality when its classifications lack a rational connection to the basis and objectives of assessment.
material_facts: The earlier land-assessment systems classified soils by quality and productivity, with rates adjusted for relevant differences in water supply or location.
The challenged scheme imposed a minimum flat assessment on dry land without regard to soil quality or productivity.

For wet land, the scheme used the size of the irrigation area to determine categories and minimum assessments, but that measure did not reliably correspond to water-supply duration, soil quality, or productivity.
In many instances, the minimum assessment exceeded the stated percentage increase over the earlier assessment.
issues.conclusion: The classifications and minimum assessments lacked a reasonable relationship to fair assessment and rationalisation of the revenue structure, so the scheme violated the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Equality permits legislative classification only when it rests on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational relation to the law’s objective. These requirements apply to fiscal laws, although legislatures receive wider latitude in tax classifications. The Court applied Article 14 and relied on Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_assessm: A party challenged the constitutionality of a scheme imposing assessments on land.
predicates.dry_land_minimum_ignores_soil_productivi: The scheme imposed a minimum assessment on dry land without taking account of differences in soil quality or productivity.
predicates.wet_land_categories_do_not_track_water_s: The scheme classified wet land using a measure that did not reliably correspond to water-supply duration, soil quality, or productivity.

issues.definition: When a land-assessment scheme is constitutionally challenged and either its dry-land minimum ignores productivity or its wet-land categories fail to track relevant differences, the assessment classification violates equality.

issues.legal_issue: A land-assessment scheme violates equality when it leaves assessment to uncontrolled official discretion without procedures enabling affected landholders to challenge material assessment decisions.
material_facts: The scheme did not prescribe a procedure for making assessments or identify the officer responsible for making them.
It provided no notice or opportunity for a landholder to contest the assessment, classification, or calculation.
The available appeal concerned notifications identifying irrigation sources, not the correctness of individual land assessments.
The State argued that existing administrative standing orders supplied the procedure, but the Court held that the statutory language did not incorporate those orders.
issues.conclusion: The scheme left assessment to arbitrary and uncontrolled discretion without an effective means to challenge its correctness, and therefore violated the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary official action as well as unreasonable statutory discrimination. A fiscal law must provide a fair and workable assessment procedure and cannot leave important assessment decisions uncontrolled. The Court applied the equality principles discussed in Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_assessm: A party challenged the constitutionality of a scheme imposing assessments on land.
predicates.assessment_officer_or_process_not_specif: The scheme did not identify the responsible assessment officer or prescribe how individual assessments were to be made.
predicates.no_effective_opportunity_to_contest_asse: Affected landholders had no effective procedure to receive notice and challenge the assessment or its material components.

issues.definition: When a land-assessment scheme is constitutionally challenged, leaves the officer or process unspecified, and gives landholders no effective opportunity to contest assessments, the scheme violates equality.
